checks.claim: Key: binary fission gives two cells with the same genes as the parent (the circular chromosome is copied first, each daughter gets a full copy)
The cell elongates (roughly doubles) and splits across its middle
checks.note: OpenStax: the cell grows and elongates, then a septum forms at midcell; 'about twice its length' is the standard simplification.

checks.claim: Some kinds divide every 20 minutes (E. coli, nutrient-rich, 37 C)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 20-60 minutes, optimal about 20 minutes.

checks.claim: Arithmetic: 20 doublings x 20 min = 400 min (6 h 40 min); 2^20 = 1,048,576, over a million in under seven hours
Wrong choices (half the genes; a new mix; one old and one new) are all wrong for fission
checks.note: Each daughter has one old and one new DNA strand (semi-conservative copying), but the GENES are the same in both, so 'one has the old genes and one has new genes' stays wrong.

checks.claim: Stem: 'keeps all of its genes on one long loop'
checks.note: Stated of this one bacterium, so it holds; many bacteria also carry small plasmid loops, and a few have linear or two chromosomes, but the stem does not claim all bacteria do.

checks.claim: Baker's yeast buds: a small bud forms on the mother cell, grows and separates
When starved, diploid yeast undergoes meiosis and forms (four haploid) spores, a sexual phase
checks.note: Trigger is chiefly nitrogen starvation with a non-fermentable carbon source; 'when food runs short' is a fair simplification.

checks.claim: Key: offspring vary, so some may suit the change
checks.note: OpenStax: in fungi sexual reproduction introduces genetic variation and often occurs in response to adverse conditions. The textbook answer.

checks.claim: Context: biologists still debate why sex persists; in yeast DNA repair may matter too
checks.note: Wikipedia (Ruderfer et al. 2006): outcrossing about once in 50,000 divisions, 'inconsistent with the idea that production of genetic variation is the main selective force'; repair is the alternative. The caveat is said, as asked.

checks.claim: Wrong choice 'Its offspring are stronger, so all survive' and context line 'sexual offspring are not stronger by rule'
checks.note: Yeast spores ARE tougher than budding cells: a thick spore wall and trehalose make them far more resistant to heat and drying, and that hardiness is a main way sporulation carries yeast through hunger. 'All survive' keeps the choice wrong, but a sharp student may see 'stronger' as half right, and the context's 'not stronger by rule' reads as denying the hardiness. Fix: change the choice to e.g. 'Its offspring are all alike, so none is weaker' or 'Its offspring need no food at all', and add to the context: 'The spores are also tough resting cells, with thick walls that outlast heat and drying, but they are not genetically better: some mixes are better and some worse.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices 'come faster' and 'copy the parent'
checks.note: Budding is the fast, copying route; sporulation is neither.

checks.claim: Key: mould on sealed bread came from airborne spores; spores are invisible and float through indoor and outdoor air
Spores settle on bread after baking, during cooling or slicing
checks.note: Baking kills spores in the dough, so contamination is after the oven.

checks.claim: Each spore grows into a new mould, a copy of the one that shed it (asexual spores)
checks.note: Airborne bread-mould spores (sporangiospores, conidia) are asexual.

checks.claim: Pier Antonio Micheli, Italian botanist (1679-1737), placed spores on melon slices, the same kind of fungus grew, and he concluded fungi do not arise by spontaneous generation (Nova plantarum genera, 1729)
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'when spores were placed on slices of melon the same type of fungi were produced that the spores came from'; also first-nature.com biography. Told as what he did and 'argued', which is suitably modest; Grokipedia's Spontaneous_generation page does not mention him and its Micheli page 404s, so this rests on Wikipedia and secondary biographies.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: bread going stale makes mould; leftover baker's yeast; bacteria turning into mould
checks.note: Staling is starch change, not life; baking kills the yeast; neither yeast nor bacteria become mould.

checks.claim: Key: runner plants are clones (genetically identical daughter plants at the nodes)
Seedlings do not come true to the parent variety
checks.note: UConn: 'the subsequent seedling plants will not develop true to the variety'. Even a self-pollinated seed would not copy the parent, since the garden strawberry is a highly mixed octoploid hybrid, so 'Both' stays wrong whatever the bees did.

checks.claim: Strawberry flowers pollinated mainly by bees
A seed forms when a (sperm) cell from a pollen grain joins an egg cell
Potato growers plant pieces with eyes (eyes are buds; clones)
Planarians are small freshwater flatworms of streams and ponds, often under stones, that glide (cilia on a mucus layer)
Key: cut across the middle, each piece regrows the missing end into a whole worm, within a few weeks
checks.note: Grokipedia: each fragment regenerates the missing anterior or posterior structures; full regeneration about 1-2 weeks. True of the usual lab species (Schmidtea, Dugesia); a few species regrow heads poorly from tail pieces, but the textbook case holds.

checks.claim: Body full of stem cells (neoblasts) that can build missing parts
checks.note: Neoblasts are 10-30 percent of cells and make nearly all body cell types; 'any missing part' is a fair grade-7 simplification.

checks.claim: A piece as small as 1/279th of a worm can regrow a whole one
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'as small as 1/279th of the original body' (T. H. Morgan's figure).

checks.claim: Some planarians reproduce by pinching in two across the middle; each half a clone
checks.note: Fission constricts at a midpoint, typically behind the pharynx.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: only the head regrows; pieces fuse back; both die
John Medley Wood found a single male Encephalartos woodii at the edge of Ngoye (oNgoye) Forest, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, in 1895
checks.note: Wikipedia: four stems of one plant 'on the fringes of a forest at oNgoye'. Wood was curator of the Durban Botanic Garden and director of the Natal Government Herbarium; 'a botanist' is fair (Grokipedia calls him botanist).

checks.claim: No other wild plant (and no female) of the kind has ever been found; extinct in the wild
Hundreds of plants (roughly 500) raised from basal shoots, all clones and males
checks.note: Wikipedia: about 500, all clones. Grokipedia gives 110-500; 'hundreds' in the stem is safe, 'roughly 500' in the context matches the usual figure.

checks.claim: Cycads have separate male and female plants; seeds form only on a female's cones from ovules reached by pollen
Kew received a shoot in 1899; its plant bore its first male cone in 2004
checks.note: Wikipedia: offset sent to Kew in 1899; 'produced, for the first time, a male cone in September 2004'.

checks.claim: Drones searched the forest in 2022 and 2024; no female found
checks.note: University of Southampton (Laura Cinti): first drone flights 2022, repeated 2024 over 195 acres of the roughly 10,000-acre forest; no female yet. The context says 'searched the forest', true though only part of it was covered.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: shoot-grown plants never make cones (false: Kew's made a cone); seeds only in home forest; still too young
checks.note: Seeds have been made by putting E. woodii pollen on females of a related species (hybrid seed), but those seeds grow on the other species' females, so 'none of them has ever made a seed' still holds.

checks.claim: Corn is wind-pollinated: pollen from the tassel to the silks
Each silk is part of one flower's pistil and connects to one ovule (a potential kernel); the pollen tube grows down the silk
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Each silk originates from a single gynoecium' and 'Each silk is connected to a single ovule at the base of the ear'.

checks.claim: Key: gaps where too little pollen reached those silks; each kernel develops only when a pollen grain lands on its silk
checks.note: UNH quote matches. Dry weather at silking and crowding can also cause poorly filled ears, but the stem points to the single row and asks 'most likely'.

checks.claim: Blocks of at least three or four short rows pollinate better than one or two long rows
checks.note: Virginia Tech: 'block plantings of at least three to four short rows will be pollinated more successfully than one or two long rows'; lists 'too few rows in a block' as a cause of poorly filled ears.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: corn needs insects (false); too much pollen (false); own-stalk pollen leaves gaps (false: maize is self-compatible, breeders self it to make inbred lines)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'self-fertilization produced homozygous lines with reduced vigor' (inbred lines by repeated selfing), so a stalk's own pollen does make kernels.

checks.claim: Key: day-blooming, red, tubular, abundant dilute nectar hidden deep, scentless = hummingbird (bird) flower
checks.note: Grokipedia: red, orange or yellow; tubular; high volumes of dilute nectar at the base of corollas; scent minimal since 'olfaction plays a lesser role in bird foraging'; nectar peaks by day.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: nectar-feeding bat (bat flowers open at night, pale or dull, strongly fruity or musty scented)
Wrong choice: night-flying moth (moth flowers pale, open at dusk or night, strong sweet scent)
Wrong choice: pollen-eating beetle (beetle flowers open bowls, strong scents, rarely nectar)
checks.note: Bees and butterflies, which do visit some red tubes, are rightly left out of the choices.

checks.claim: Context: syndromes are tendencies, not rules; bees visit some red flowers too
checks.note: Cane and Dunne 2014: generalist bees pollinate red-flowered Penstemon eatonii. Grokipedia: only about 30 percent of species match their predicted pollinators closely.

checks.claim: Meadow buttercup's nectar guide is visible only in ultraviolet: a darker centre where the nectaries are
checks.note: Wikipedia: 'visible only when viewed in ultraviolet light'; 'a darker center, where the nectaries are located'. UV photographs of Ranunculus acris show bright petals with a UV-dark centre (a bullseye), matching 'pale at its tip and dark toward the centre'.

checks.claim: Key: the pattern guides bees to the nectar (bees see UV; nectar guides cut handling time)
checks.note: USFS: 'a region of low ultraviolet reflectance near the center of each petal ... helps a bee quickly locate the flower's center'. Buttercups are also visited by flies and beetles, but bees are the textbook UV case and the key says 'most likely'.

checks.claim: Context: bees cannot see red; bee flowers often blue or yellow
checks.note: USFS quote 'bees cannot see red'. Strictly, bees have no red receptor, so red looks dark to them; the simplification is standard and still true at this grade.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: warns leaf-eaters; draws moths at night; soaks up light to make food
checks.note: UV-absorbing petal pigments may also shade pollen from sunlight (a sunscreen role studied in some species), but making food is not it, and buttercups are day flowers; none of the wrong choices is defensible.

checks.claim: Context: a plant makes its food in its green leaves, not its petals
checks.note: Green stems photosynthesize a little too, but yellow petals do not make the plant's food.

checks.claim: Key: the ovary grows into the pod; a fruit is the mature ovary; ovules become seeds
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the mature ovary of a flowering plant (angiosperm) that develops after fertilization'; seeds 'derived from the ovules'.

checks.claim: A pea pod is a dry fruit (legume) that splits to release its seeds; peas joined by a short stalk
checks.note: The pod splits along its seam ('a dehiscent fruit'); each pea hangs on a short stalk (the funiculus).

checks.claim: Tomatoes and cucumbers are botanically fruits though cooks call them vegetables
Wrong choices: petals (draw pollinators), stamens (make pollen), sepals (wrap the bud); none becomes the pod
checks.note: In a pea the dry sepals stay at the base of the pod, but they do not form it. (Garden peas mostly pollinate themselves before the flower opens; the context's 'petals draw pollinators' is said of petals in general and stays true.)

unit_notes: Plant- and microbe-led throughout; no question touches human reproduction (animal sperm and eggs appear only in the writer's fact sheet, F3). One uncertain: the yeast question's 'stronger' wrong choice and its context line, since yeast spores really are tougher (heat- and drought-resistant) than budding cells. The Micheli melon-slice experiment rests on Wikipedia and secondary biographies and is told modestly ('argued'). Wood's cycad figures (about 500 clones, Kew 1899 and 2004, drones 2022 and 2024) check out; the 500 figure varies by source (Grokipedia 110-500), and the stem's 'hundreds' is safe.
